clip_narrations: Yale, nineteen sixty-one. A volunteer faces thirty switches, from fifteen up to four hundred fifty volts. A man in a grey coat says, please continue.
Through the wall, the learner pounded, then went silent. Still, twenty-six of forty men pressed on to the last switch. For their brains, this was a total nightmare.
Before the test, fourteen Yale students guessed how many people would go all the way. Their average guess was about one in a hundred.
The secret was the setup. The draw was rigged, so he was always the teacher. The learner was in on it. Only the teacher felt a real shock.
Instead of blind obedience, look closer. Told the experiment requires it, men went on, but told you have no other choice, they stopped.
First, he put the learner right in the same room. Seeing the man struggle up close, only forty percent went to the end.
Next, the teacher had to press the learner's hand onto a shock plate himself. Now only thirty percent went all the way.
Finally, when two other teachers in the room refused to flip the switches, thirty-six out of forty men stood up and stopped too.
In two thousand nine, a new study stopped at one hundred fifty volts. Seventy percent tried to keep going. The researchers were left completely stunned.
Which is why a calm voice saying it is for a good cause is so powerful. Across all his versions, most people stopped, and you can too.
